query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of tin (Sn) to equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will improve its resistance to oxygen attack at high temperatures by promoting the formation of a more adherent, protective oxide scale, while maintaining its favorable room‐ and high‐temperature mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr with a single BCC solid solution showing 8–16% room‐temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C under strain rates of 10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(-1).
generation.intervention: Incorporate a trace amount (e.g., around 2 atomic %) of Sn into the alloy composition during melting/casting.
generation.conditions: Perform oxidation tests in air at 800 °C for 5 hours under similar strain rate conditions used in previous high-temperature tests, while also evaluating room temperature mechanical properties to ensure performance preservation.
generation.structural_mediator: The Sn addition is expected to segregate to the alloy surface during high-temperature exposure, leading to the formation of a continuous, Sn-enriched oxide scale (such as SnO2 or a mixed oxide layer) that adheres strongly to the substrate.
generation.mechanism: Tin acts as a reactive element that modifies the oxidation process by enhancing scale adhesion and reducing oxygen diffusion through the surface, thereby suppressing pest oxidation without adversely affecting the intrinsic mechanical properties of the alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, the Sn-doped variant is predicted to show significantly reduced pesting (disintegration due to oxidation) and improved scale integrity after a 5-hour air exposure at 800 °C, while retaining similar room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.baseline: The untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits inadequate oxygen resistance (pest oxidation) during high-temperature oxidation, despite good mechanical performance at room temperature and 1000 °C.
generation.boundary: This intervention is anticipated to be effective under air exposure at approximately 800 °C for durations on the order of 5 hours; its performance under significantly different temperatures, longer exposure times, or varying strain rates remains to be determined.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Sn concentration and its influence on potential secondary phase formation are not fully defined; effects on very long-term oxidation and creep properties outside the tested temperature/time range require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples using the same casting protocol: one with the standard equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr composition and one with an additional ~2 at% Sn. Expose both sets to air at 800 °C for 5 hours. Characterize the surface oxide scales (via SEM/EDS and XRD), measure weight gains, and assess mechanical properties (room-temperature tensile tests and high-temperature yield strength tests) before and after exposure.
measurements: Surface oxide morphology and phase composition (SEM, EDS, XRD)
Room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Sn-doped alloy does not demonstrate significantly improved oxidation resistance (e.g., similar or higher mass gain, evidence of pest oxidation, poor oxide scale adhesion) compared to the undoped alloy, or if its mechanical properties deteriorate beyond acceptable limits, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Senkov et al. [] conducted compression tests on Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 at room temperature as well as at 600 °C, 800 °C, 1000 °C and 1200 °C under different strain rates and used Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) to investigate the microstructural changes during the deformation process and the fracture mechanisms. These researchers claimed that the above temperature range can be divided into three regions, each one characterized by different deformation behavior. According to Senkov et al. [], at temperatures up to 600 °C twinning compensates for restricted dislocation mobility. At 800 °C Grain Boundary Sliding (GBS) is not yet supported by sufficient dislocation mobility and diffusion leads to cavitation at grain boundaries, while at 1000–1200 °C cavitation at grain boundaries disappears and Dynamic Recrystallization (DRX) occurs. DRX processes are assumed to be responsible for the rapid drop in the flow stress after yielding followed by a steady state flow. The compression test data for Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 at room temperature include compression yield strength of 929 MPa [] and 1073 MPa [] together with fracture strain higher than 50% []. Structural metallic materials for applications at high temperatures must have a balance of mechanical properties and oxidation resistance. Coated and internally cooled Ni-based superalloys are used in gas turbine engines close to their high temperature limit, which is imposed by the melting temperature of Ni. The search for new alloys with similar or better capabilities at higher temperatures has concentrated on Nb-silicide based alloys that have lower densities, significantly higher solidus temperatures in excess of 1900 °C and can offer notable mechanical properties []. For example, some of these alloys can have compressive yield strength of about 1800 MPa at room temperature, 1200 MPa at 1000 °C and 500 MPa at 1200 °C []. The oxidation resistance of Nb-silicide based alloys was improved dramatically when the key alloying elements Al, Cr, Si, and Ti were in synergy with other transition and refractory metals, for example Hf, Mo, and simple metal and metalloid elements, e.g., Sn [,,,,]. In the case of Sn, the early research [,] concentrated on alloys where its concentration was low to avoid the formation of the A15-Nb3Sn compound. In 2007, Geng et al [] reported that the addition

The research on the oxidation of Nb-silicide-based alloys would suggest (a) that Ge and/or Sn are needed to suppress pest oxidation, and (b) that, when these alloying additions were present individually or simultaneously in the alloys, the spallation of their scales at high temperatures was not suppressed. It is now well established that Ge or Sn has an effect on macrosegregation and can also reduce the liquidus temperature of the alloy. Alloying with Sn can affect the stability of the Nbss but not the alloying with Ge, which can, however, significantly reduce the cracking of the substrate below the scale/substrate interface []. Unfortunately, from the oxidation research on multicomponent Nb-silicide-based alloys, it is not clear whether it was the synergy of Sn or Ge individually or simultaneously with Al, Cr, Si, and Ti that improved oxidation resistance, or whether the presence of oxygen scavenging Hf with/without transition and refractory metals and with some or all of the aforementioned elements was essential for increasing the oxidation resistance.
